extracted.intended_audience: practitioners before the USPTO, counsel in USPTO disciplinary proceedings, and OED staff
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural requirements used by the USPTO Office of Enrollment and Discipline and the Administrative Law Judge to evaluate practitioner misconduct, determine liability, and impose sanctions, plus the pre-hearing and hearing submission rules for disciplinary hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors for imposing sanctions (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider the following four factors: (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to a client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner’s misconduct; and (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court often looks to the ABA’s Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when determining aggravating or mitigating factors. Aggravating factors can include dishonest or selfish motive; mitigating factors can include no prior disciplinary record, remorse, and personal problems contributing to misconduct. The totality of these factors informs the severity of the sanction (e.g., suspension length, probation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowingly neglecting client matters constitutes failure to act with reasonable diligence. Examples: filing an application but failing to take further necessary steps (e.g., remit fees, file inventor’s oath), or doing nothing to advance a client's cause. Case law cited illustrates failures to pursue or cure defaults as misconduct. The timing alone may not prove misconduct without showing lack of diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to keep clients informed and to explain matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3),(4) & (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter, promptly comply with reasonable requests for information, and explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit clients to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to respond to repeated client inquiries, concealing adverse status (e.g., that an application went abandoned), or affirmatively misrepresenting the status are violations. Examples and state bar decisions are used to determine when lack of communication rises to misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misconduct: dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affirmative misrepresentations to a client about filing status (stating everything is filed when required items were not filed) are actionable misconduct. Such misrepresentations weigh heavily toward a severe sanction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to cooperate with OED investigations / failure to respond to lawful demands (37 C.F.R. § 11.801(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not fail to cooperate with the OED in an investigation or knowingly fail to respond to a lawful demand or request for information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Knowingly' is defined by 37 C.F.R. § 11.1 as having actual knowledge. Failure to respond to an RFI, providing evasive answers, or not producing requested documents supports a finding of non-cooperation and can be prejudicial to the administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping — maintain readily accessible accounting records (37 C.F.R. § 11.115(f)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must maintain certain accounting records and ensure they are readily accessible to the practitioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Records stored off-site must nevertheless be readily accessible and producible/printable upon request. The Order references § 11.115(f)(1) for the specific records required (receipt and disbursement journals, ledger records, retainer agreements, client accounts, bills, disbursement records, bank records, quarterly reconciliations, etc.). Keeping records in storage without a mechanism to produce them when requested supports a violation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof — clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; Respondent bears the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear and convincing is an intermediate standard between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt, requiring evidence 'of such weight that it produces in the mind of the trier of fact a firm belief or conviction' as to the truth of the allegations. Case law definitions and citations are cited to explain the standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary judgment standard applied in USPTO disciplinary cases (Rule 56-type standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motions for summary judgment in USPTO disciplinary proceedings are governed by the standard used in Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 56: summary judgment is appropriate when there is no genuine, triable issue of material fact and under governing law there can be but one reasonable conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An issue is 'genuine' only if a reasonable factfinder could rule for either party; a fact is 'material' if it could affect the outcome under governing law. The Court may grant summary judgment on liability but reserve the sanction determination for hearing if material issues remain on sanction factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of USPTO disciplinary jurisdiction (37 C.F.R. § 11.19(a) & § 11.5(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's disciplinary authority extends to all practitioners engaged in practice before it; 'practice before the Office' includes law-related services connected with presentation to the Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A person need not be a registered patent practitioner to be subject to the USPTO's disciplinary jurisdiction if they provide legal services before the Office (e.g., prepared and filed an application). Denials of registration are not material to jurisdiction if practice before the Office is established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-hearing and hearing procedural requirements (notice, hearing, discovery limits, exhibits, witnesses, motions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners alleged to have committed misconduct must receive notice and opportunity for a hearing (35 U.S.C. § 32; 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.39, 11.44). The Order prescribes pretrial and hearing procedures (deadlines for conferral, witness lists with summaries, exhibit lists and electronic exhibits, format requirements, objections, pre-hearing statements, and motion practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key procedural rules and logistics: discovery is not authorized absent court order (37 C.F.R. § 11.52); electronic exhibits must be OCR'd PDF on CD-ROM; parties should submit joint exhibits (JNT #); provide hardcopy indexed binders with numbered tabs; file objections and responses by specified deadlines; pre-hearing statements must list issues, stipulated facts, disputed facts, applicable law, estimated time, and conclusions; meet-and-confer required before filing motions (37 C.F.R. § 11.43). Motions in limine and response deadlines are set in the Order and failure to timely respond to motions may be deemed a waiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility/usage of settlement communications (37 C.F.R. § 11.26)
rubrics_metrics.description: Offers of compromise and statements made during settlement discussions shall not be admissible in subsequent proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may not rely on prior settlement negotiations or disclosed agreed sanctions as evidence on summary judgment or in determining sanctions; the Court will redact such content to avoid undue influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions by failure to deny allegations (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Every allegation in the complaint that is not denied by a respondent in the answer shall be deemed to be admitted and may be considered proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondents must specifically admit or deny each allegation. Denials that are conclusory or unsupported do not raise a genuine dispute of material fact under summary judgment standards; bare denials without evidence will be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and effect of 'prejudicial to the administration of justice' (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice is professional misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to cooperate with investigation, evasive responses to RFIs, or conduct undermining self-regulation and public confidence in the profession are examples. Court and Federal Circuit precedent (e.g., Bender v. Dudas) show that evasive responses to USPTO inquiries can be prejudicial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of comparative authority and case law to interpret USPTO Rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions of state bars adopting the ABA Model Rules and other courts are used as persuasive authority in interpreting USPTO disciplinary rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO Rules were modeled on the ABA Model Rules; state bar disciplinary decisions and relevant federal case law are cited to interpret duties (e.g., diligence, communication) and sanctions.
